extracted.intended_audience: litigators and judges handling patent §101 motions (district court practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards for deciding patent eligibility challenges under 35 U.S.C. § 101 at the Rule 12(c)/12(b)(6) pleading stage, including use of the Alice/Mayo two-step framework, representative-claim practice, and when claim construction or factual development is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 12(c) standard for judgment on the pleadings
rubrics_metrics.description: In considering a motion for judgment on the pleadings, the Court 'must accept the truth of all factual allegations in the complaint and must draw all reasonable inferences in favor of the non-movant.' A motion can be granted 'only if no relief could be granted under any set of facts that could be proved.' The purpose is to dispose of claims where the material facts are undisputed and judgment can be entered on the competing pleadings and exhibits thereto.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Revell v. Port Auth., Turbe v. Gov't of Virgin Islands, Venetec Int’l, Inc. v. Nexus Med., LLC. Emphasizes that the movant must show that no plausible set of facts would entitle the non-movant to relief; factual inferences drawn for non-movant at pleading stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent-eligibility is a legal question based on underlying facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101 is a question of law, based on underlying facts. Eligibility disputes can be resolved on a Rule 12(b)(6) or Rule 12(c) motion 'where the undisputed facts, considered under the standards required by that Rule, require a holding of ineligibility under the substantive standards of law.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Aatrix Software, Berkheimer, SAP Am. v. InvestPic and other Federal Circuit precedent. Reminds courts to identify whether underlying factual disputes exist that would preclude resolution at the pleading stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice/Mayo two-step framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the two-step Alice/Mayo framework: Step 1 — determine whether the claims are drawn to a patent-ineligible concept (e.g., an abstract idea) by examining the focus and character of the claim as a whole. Step 2 — if directed to an ineligible concept, examine the claim elements individually and as an ordered combination to determine whether there is an 'inventive concept' sufficient to ensure the patent amounts to significantly more than a patent on the ineligible concept itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotes Alice and Mayo. Emphasizes the need to look both to the claim's overall character and to additional elements that might transform an abstract idea into a patent-eligible application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice Step One — focus on specific asserted improvement vs abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: At step one, courts consider whether the focus of the claims is on 'the specific asserted improvement in computer capabilities . . . or, instead, on a process that qualifies as an 'abstract idea' for which computers are invoked merely as a tool.' Claims that focus on a result/effect and merely invoke generic processes are likely directed to an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Enfish, Finjan, McRO. Courts should assess the claim's 'character as a whole' and determine whether the claimed invention improves computer technology itself or instead implements a longstanding practice using a computer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice Step Two — inventive concept must be more than routine or conventional
rubrics_metrics.description: At step two, additional claim elements must provide an inventive concept beyond the abstract idea; they are insufficient if they are 'well-understood, routine, conventional activities' or merely generic computer components. A claim that simply states the abstract idea and adds 'apply it' fails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotes Alice and Mayo. Uses examples where generic computer implementations failed (Ultramercial, buySAFE, OIP Techs.). Reminds that the inquiry examines elements individually and as an ordered combination to see if they 'transform the nature of the claim.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative-claim practice and burdens
rubrics_metrics.description: A court may limit its § 101 analysis to representative claims when the claims at issue are 'substantially similar and linked to the same ineligible concept.' The patent challenger asserting representativeness bears the initial burden of making a prima facie showing that the group of claims are substantially similar and linked to the same ineligible concept; if made, the burden shifts to the patent owner to demonstrate why the representative claim is not decisive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Mobile Acuity, Berkheimer. If the patentee cannot make a non-frivolous argument against representativeness, it's precluded from arguing eligibility of other claims in the group.

rubrics_metrics.name: When claims should be treated as representative (patentee's failure to distinguish)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may treat a claim as representative 'if the patentee does not present any meaningful argument for the distinctive significance of any claim limitations not found in the representative claim or if the parties agree to treat a claim as representative.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rule: if patentee fails to articulate a meaningful differentiation of dependent or other independent claims from the representative claim in the record/pleadings, the court can treat the representative claim as dispositive for the group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of claim construction in § 101 analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Although claim construction is not a prerequisite to a § 101 determination, eligibility analysis 'requires a full understanding of the basic character of the claimed subject matter' and it is often desirable—and often necessary—to resolve claim construction disputes prior to a § 101 analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Content Extraction, Bancorp Services. Courts may proceed without formal construction when claim meaning is obvious from the patent and record, but should avoid ruling on § 101 when disputed constructions could alter the outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of precedent to identify 'abstract ideas' (targeted advertising example)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit has repeatedly held that targeted advertising and information tailoring (e.g., collecting/using viewing history to recommend content, tailoring ads by time of day) are abstract concepts not patentable under § 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Broadband iTV, Free Stream Media, Intellectual Ventures I. This provides a precedent-based rubric: if claims are materially similar to those ruled abstract in precedent, that weighs toward ineligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer components do not make an abstract idea patent-eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that merely apply an abstract idea using generic computer components (e.g., 'a computer', 'a manager', 'a delivery module') or that add routine data storage/selection/measurement steps are not transformed into an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and citations include OIP Techs., Ultramercial, Customedia. The Court should scrutinize whether claimed components are 'non-generic' and how they change computer functionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent-claim specificity: minor structural or functional additions may be insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Dependent claims that add only minor structural or functional features—storing user profiles, using different types of data, sending a delivery plan or product catalog, specifying client device types—may still be 'substantially similar' to an abstract representative claim and fail to transform the claim into patent-eligible subject matter if they lack specificity or inventive technical detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical analysis: group dependent claims by added features and evaluate whether any added limitation meaningfully improves computer functionality or is merely generic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual disputes about conventionality or novelty preclude judgment on pleadings
rubrics_metrics.description: If there are underlying factual questions (e.g., whether an asserted component is 'well-understood, routine, or conventional' or whether an architecture is novel/non-generic), those factual disputes can preclude resolving § 101 at the pleading stage and make judgment on the pleadings improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Revell, BSG Tech, Turbe. The court should deny a Rule 12(c) motion where factual development (discovery, claim construction) is needed to resolve whether elements supply an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court should avoid § 101 dismissal when claim meaning is contested and could be dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: When a plaintiff articulates a specific claim construction issue (e.g., meaning of 'social connections') that could affect whether claims are directed to an abstract idea or whether they improve computer functionality, the court should defer § 101 ruling until after claim construction and factual development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites the court's practice and cases (e.g., Execware v. BJ’s) declining to decide § 101 where claim construction could change the outcome; admonishes against adopting a construction at pleading stage that may be unfavorable and later prove incorrect.
